x.ASV: I love Jehovah, because he heareth My voice and my supplications.
x.Darby: I love Jehovah, for he hath heard my voice [and] my supplications;
x.KJV: I love the Lord, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications.
x.YLT: I have loved, because Jehovah heareth My voice, my supplication,

nt: Here, **my voice** represents the psalmist’s prayers and requests. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh hears me]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [because Yahweh hears my pleas]

x.ASV: Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, Therefore will I call upon him as long as I live.
x.Darby: For he hath inclined his ear unto me, and I will call upon him during [all] my days.
x.KJV: Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live.
x.YLT: Because He hath inclined His ear to me, And during my days I call.

nt: The psalmist is using **he extends his ear to me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he listens to me” or “he pays attention to what I say.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he pays attention to what I say]
The psalmist is using the term **days** to refer to his lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and throughout my lifetime]

The psalmist assumes that readers will understand that **I will call out** means he will call out to Yahweh. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will call out to Yahweh]

x.ASV: The cords of death compassed me, And the pains of Sheol gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow.
x.Darby: The bands of death encompassed me, and the anguish of Sheol took hold of me; I found trouble and sorrow:
x.KJV: The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow.
x.YLT: Compassed me have cords of death, And straits of Sheol have found me, Distress and sorrow I find.

nt: These two phrases **The cords of death surrounded me** and **the constrictions of Sheol found me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The cords of death surrounded me, indeed, the constrictions of Sheol found me]

Here the psalmist is picturing death as if it were **cords** that could wrap around and bind someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It seemed that I would die soon]

Here David is speaking of **the constrictions of Sheol** as if they were ropes or chains that could physically grip and restrain him. He means that he felt as though he was very close to dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I felt as though I were dying]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anguish** and **sorrow**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [I was anguished and sorrowful]

x.ASV: Then called I upon the name of Jehovah: O Jehovah, I beseech thee, deliver my soul.
x.Darby: Then called I upon the name of Jehovah: I beseech thee, Jehovah, deliver my soul.
x.KJV: Then called I upon the name of the Lord; O Lord, I beseech thee, deliver my soul.
x.YLT: And in the name of Jehovah I call: I pray Thee, O Jehovah, deliver my soul,

nt: The psalmist is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then I called on Yahweh]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [I beg you to rescue my life]

Here, **life** represents the person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [rescue me] or [keep me from dying]

x.ASV: Gracious is Jehovah, and righteous; Yea, our God is merciful.
x.Darby: Gracious is Jehovah and righteous; and ourGod is merciful.
x.KJV: Gracious is the Lord, and righteous; yea, our God is merciful.
x.YLT: Gracious is Jehovah, and righteous, Yea, our God is merciful,

nt: Here **and** introduces not an addition but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, our God, is also compassionate]

x.ASV: Jehovah preserveth the simple: I was brought low, and he saved me.
x.Darby: Jehovah keepeth the simple: I was brought low, and he saved me.
x.KJV: The Lord preserveth the simple: I was brought low, and he helped me.
x.YLT: A preserver of the simple is Jehovah, I was low, and to me He giveth salvation.

nt: The psalmist is using the adjective **naive** as a noun to refer to people who are inexperienced or who cannot care for themselves. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who cannot care for themselves]

Here the psalmist is speaking of his difficult circumstances as if he were physically **low**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I was in a bad way] or [I was in trouble]

x.ASV: Return unto thy rest, O my soul; For Jehovah hath dealt bountifully with thee.
x.Darby: Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for Jehovah hath dealt bountifully with thee.
x.KJV: Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee.
x.YLT: Turn back, O my soul, to thy rest, For Jehovah hath conferred benefits on thee.

nt: שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁ⁠י לִ⁠מְנוּחָ֑יְ⁠כִי כִּֽי־יְ֝הוָ֗ה גָּמַ֥ל עָלָֽיְ⁠כִי
The psalmist is speaking to himself in the second person as **your** and **you**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in first person as modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual/emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I must return myself to calmness]
By **rest**, the psalmist means “a state of restfulness.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Return to your state of restfulness]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s good deeds as if they were **repaid** like a debt or wages. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh has done good things for you] or [for Yahweh has done good things for me]

x.ASV: For thou hast delivered my soul from death, Mine eyes from tears, And my feet from falling.
x.Darby: For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, my feet from falling.
x.KJV: For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.
x.YLT: For Thou hast delivered my soul from death, My eyes from tears, my feet from overthrowing.

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

Here, **my soul** represents the psalmist himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [For you rescued me from death]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **death**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For you rescued my soul from dying]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **eye**, to mean all of him in the act of weeping. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me from weeping]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **foot**, to mean all of him in the act of stumbling or falling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me from stumbling]

x.ASV: I will walk before Jehovah In the land of the living.
x.Darby: I will walk before Jehovah in the land of the living.
x.KJV: I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living.
x.YLT: I walk habitually before Jehovah In the lands of the living.

nt: Here the psalmist is speaking as if he were literally walking **to the face of Yahweh**. He means that he will live in a way that acknowledges Yahweh in all that he does. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will acknowledge Yahweh in all that I do]

The psalmist is using **to the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the presence of” or “before.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

The psalmist is using **in the lands of the living** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as long as I am alive” or “during my lifetime.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as long as I live]

x.ASV: I believe, for I will speak: I was greatly afflicted:
x.Darby: I believed, therefore have I spoken. As for me, I was greatly afflicted.
x.KJV: I believed, therefore have I spoken: I was greatly afflicted:
x.YLT: I have believed, for I speak, I--I have been afflicted greatly.

nt: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I trusted Yahweh]

The implication is that the psalmist was speaking to himself or to God about his distress. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [though I said to myself]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** twice, even though it is not necessary for understanding. He is doing that to emphasize his personal distress and suffering. If a speaker of your language would use repeated pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [woe is me; I am very wretched]

x.ASV: I said in my haste, All men are liars.
x.Darby: I said in my haste, All men are liars.
x.KJV: I said in my haste, All men are liars.
x.YLT: I said in my haste, `Every man is a liar.'

nt: The pronoun **I** is stated twice for emphasis. The psalmist is emphasizing that he himself was the one who made this statement. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [As for me, I said]

By **I, I said**, the psalmist means that he said this to himself or thought this to himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, I said to myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **panic**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I was panicking]

x.ASV: What shall I render unto Jehovah For all his benefits toward me?
x.Darby: What shall I render unto Jehovah, [for] all his benefits toward me?
x.KJV: What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me?
x.YLT: What do I return to Jehovah? All His benefits are upon me.

nt: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is not possible for me to return to Yahweh all of his bestowments to me.]

The implication is that the psalmist cannot fully repay Yahweh for all his goodness. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [How can I pay back to Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bestowments**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything that he has done to be kind to me]

x.ASV: I will take the cup of salvation, And call upon the name of Jehovah.
x.Darby: I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of Jehovah.
x.KJV: I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord.
x.YLT: The cup of salvation I lift up, And in the name of Jehovah I call.

nt: This is probably a reference to a drink offering, which was a sacrifice that involved pouring wine on the altar, and which the psalmist will offer as a grateful response to Yahweh for saving him. The full meaning of this statement can be made explicit. Alternate translation: [I will present a drink offering to Yahweh because he saved me]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and call on Yahweh]

x.ASV: I will pay my vows unto Jehovah, Yea, in the presence of all his people.
x.Darby: I will perform my vows unto Jehovah, yea, before all his people.
x.KJV: I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all his people.
x.YLT: My vows to Jehovah let me complete, I pray you, before all His people.

nt: The implication is that these are people who have gathered to worship Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the people who have gathered to worship him]

x.ASV: Precious in the sight of Jehovah Is the death of his saints.
x.Darby: Precious in the sight of Jehovah is the death of his saints.
x.KJV: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
x.YLT: Precious in the eyes of Jehovah is the death for His saints.

nt: The word **Precious** here does not imply that Yahweh desires the death of his faithful ones, but that the death of his saints is costly to him and grieves him. See how you translated a similar expression in [Psalm 72:14](../072/014.md). Alternate translation: [Yahweh considers the death of his faithful ones to be a costly thing]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **death**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When one of his faithful people dies, that grieves Yahweh very much]

The psalmist is using **in the eyes of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh’s judgment]

The psalmist is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [is the death of any of his faithful people]

x.ASV: O Jehovah, truly I am thy servant: I am thy servant, the son of thy handmaid; Thou hast loosed my bonds.
x.Darby: Yea, Jehovah! for I am thy servant; I am thy servant, the son of thy handmaid: thou hast loosed my bonds.
x.KJV: O Lord, truly I am thy servant; I am thy servant, and the son of thine handmaid: thou hast loosed my bonds.
x.YLT: Cause it to come, O Jehovah, for I am Thy servant. I am Thy servant, son of Thy handmaid, Thou hast opened my bonds.

nt: The psalmist here switches to second person by saying **your servant**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue using third person as in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Indeed, for I am Yahweh’s servant; I am his servant, the son of his servant woman; he has undone my bonds]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [definitely I am your servant]

The phrase **the son of your servant woman** adds to the meaning of **I am your servant**. In the culture of the time, the son of a servant woman was a permanent servant, without the right to go free after six years. See [Exodus 21:2–4](../../exo/21/02.md). You could include this information if it would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I am your permanent servant, the son of your servant woman]

Here the psalmist is speaking of his troubles as if they were **bonds** that tied him up and prevented him from moving freely. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you have freed me from my troubles]

x.ASV: I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, And will call upon the name of Jehovah.
x.Darby: I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and will call upon the name of Jehovah.
x.KJV: I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and will call upon the name of the Lord.
x.YLT: To Thee I sacrifice a sacrifice of thanks, And in the name of Jehovah I call.

nt: The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I will make a sacrifice to you to thank you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will make a sacrifice to you to thank you]

Here, **name** represents the person of Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will call out to Yahweh]

x.ASV: I will pay my vows unto Jehovah, Yea, in the presence of all his people,
x.Darby: I will perform my vows unto Jehovah, yea, before all his people,
x.KJV: I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all his people,
x.YLT: My vows to Jehovah let me complete, I pray you, before all His people,

nt: See how you translated this in [verse 14](../116/014.md).

The psalmist says **right in front of all of his people** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [right in front of a gathering of his people]

x.ASV: In the courts of Jehovah’s house, In the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Praise ye Jehovah.
x.Darby: In the courts of Jehovah's house, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Hallelujah!
x.KJV: In the courts of the Lord’s house, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Praise ye the Lord.
x.YLT: In the courts of the house of Jehovah, In thy midst, O Jerusalem, praise ye Jah!

nt: The psalmist is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking to **Jerusalem** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about his commitment to worship and praise God in the holy city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [in the midst of Jerusalem]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
